title: Autocorrelated Arrival Benchmark Diary (scratch)
summary: Personal scratchpad for a set of latency/throughput experiments using autocorrelated arrival traces (AR(1) style). Focus: p95/p99 behavior under sustained correlated burstiness vs Poisson baseline, effect of warming and KV-cache priming, and scheduler backpressure response.
content:
Purpose
- Explore how autocorrelated inter-arrival times (AR(1) with rho in [0.6,0.95]) change tail-latency compared to Poisson arrivals at same mean QPS.
- Validate that small persistent correlations cause runway buildup in request queueing and show different effectiveness of prefix-KV cache priming.

Environment / harness
- Testbed: single-host Dedicated-like node (4x A100 40GB), but runs pinned to 1 GPU for deterministic interference.
- Model: open-13b-q4 (sharded), sequence length 128, generation max 64, typical prompt tokens 40-60.
- Runtime: local bench harness (bench/arrival-sim v0.9.1), dynamic batching enabled, max batch size 32, batching deadline 8ms, preemption disabled.
- Warm state: two modes: warm (run a warmup traffic wave 30s before measurement), cold (empty kv caches + restarted model server).

Arrival generator notes
- AR(1) inter-arrival formulation: x_t = mu + rho*(x_{t-1}-mu) + eps_t, eps ~ Exp(lambda) to keep positive inter-arrivals.
- Target mean QPS: 80 (mean inter-arrival 12.5ms) for baseline. Ran sweeps at 60, 80, 100 QPS.
- rho values: 0 (approx Poisson), 0.6, 0.8, 0.92. Correlated blocks show longer sequences of short inter-arrivals (bursts) and longer gaps.

Key runs (timestamps local)
- 2025-06-18 10:15: baseline Poisson 80 QPS, warm. 30s warmup + 5min measurement.
- 2025-06-18 11:00: AR rho=0.6, 80 QPS, warm.
- 2025-06-18 11:45: AR rho=0.8, 80 QPS, warm + primed KV (prefix cache seeded).
- 2025-06-19 09:20: AR rho=0.92, 80 QPS, cold restart. 10min measurement to observe longer tail drift.
- 2025-06-20 14:00: Sweep across QPS 60/80/100 for rho=0.8, warm vs cold.

Metrics snapshot (representative)
- Captured: p50, p90, p95, p99, p999 (ms); mean throughput (QPS); dropped requests; max queue depth.

Observations / quick analysis
- Even modest rho (~0.6) increases p95/p99 substantially despite same mean QPS — queueing amplification.
- Higher rho creates long-tail events where batching accumulates but then drains causing long p999 spikes.
- Warm+primed KV reduces median and p90 by ~10-20% in r3 vs equivalent cold, but does not fully mitigate p99/p999 when rho >= 0.8. Suggests cache helps single-request latency but burst coalescence still overwhelms scheduling/backpressure.
- At 100 QPS (r5) system shows significant drops and sustained backlog: scheduler didn't adapt quickly enough to maintain SLOs. Batching deadline of 8ms can make latency worse if many requests queue for batch formation during bursts.

Hypotheses
- Prefix/KV cache helps per-token cost and happy-path latency, but autocorrelated bursts expose weaknesses in fairness and queue-thinning policies.
- A dynamic batching deadline (adaptive based on recent inter-arrival variance) could reduce p99 without sacrificing throughput.
- Fast preemption or fractional batching (process partially-full batch quickly during long queues) may lower p999 spikes.

Quick notes on instrumentation gaps
- Need finer-grained per-token timings (time-to-first-token vs full completion). Current harness only logs end-to-end completion.
- Telemetry: correlate scheduler queue depth with per-request kv cache hit flag to see if cache misses align with tails.
- Missing: GC/OS preemption traces for cold restart runs — could be contributing to extreme p999 in r4.

Next steps / TODOs
- Re-run r3 with adaptive batching: deadline = f(variance of last 200 inter-arrivals), baseline: clamp 2–12ms. Compare p95/p99. (Assign: Ravi)
- Add per-token / TTF token logging in bench harness (Assign: me).
- Try fractional batching experiment: allow a batch to be dispatched when oldest request > 20ms in queue, even if under max batch size.
- Run multi-GPU pinned runs to see if shard contention amplifies these effects (smaller scope: single-GPU first).

Scratch timeline (notes while running)
- r2: saw queue depth steadily climb to ~20 over 90s then oscillate; server CPU on host stayed low which suggests GPU-side backlog.
- r4 cold: 3x p999 relative to warm runs; after ~4min tail gradually reduced as cache warmed and scheduler regained equilibrium.
- r5: dropped started at minute 2; when drops happen, p50/p90 oscillation becomes noisier indicating partial overload rather than graceful degradation.

Loose ASCII sketch of burst waveform (for my memory)
- timeline: |---quiet(120ms)---(burst: 6 req at 10ms gaps)---quiet(200ms)---(burst)---|
- autocorr makes these clusters stick together, Poisson does not.

Closing thought
- This feels like a classic queueing + autocorrelation pathology: mean QPS masks burstiness. For product SLOs we should prioritize p99 engineered defenses (adaptive deadline, fractional dispatch, better backpressure) rather than only tuning mean throughput.

Attachments I wanted to save separately
- raw perf logs (bench-run-r3.tar.gz) -> upload to GCS and link in linked_artifacts when available.
- quick flamegraphs for r4 (GC suspicion).
conclusions: Autocorrelation significantly increases tail latency even at same mean QPS.
KV priming improves medians but cannot fully prevent long-tail due to scheduler/queueing effects.
Adaptive batching deadlines and fractional dispatch are promising mitigations to test next.
